entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alfred Sao-ke Sze (born c. 1877, died 1958) emerged as a pivotal figure in Chinese diplomacy during the tumultuous transition from the Qing Dynasty to the Republic of China, navigating the complexities of international relations as China sought to assert its sovereignty and modernize its statecraft. A Yale-educated scholar and statesman, Sze represented China on the global stage through two World Wars and the interwar period, engaging with major international bodies and powers to advocate for his nation's interests amidst imperialist pressures and domestic upheaval. His career spanned key ambassadorships and delegate roles, positioning him as a central architect of modern Chinese foreign policy, particularly concerning Western powers.

Sze's diplomatic career was marked by significant appointments, including serving as Ambassador to the United States (1921–1929, 1931–1933) and the United Kingdom (1929–1931, 1933–1938). He played a crucial role as a delegate to the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, where he vociferously protested the transfer of German concessions in Shandong to Japan, and later at the Washington Naval Conference (1921–1922), where he secured the Nine-Power Treaty affirming China's territorial integrity. His tenure also included representing China at the League of Nations, where he championed collective security and China's rights against Japanese aggression in Manchuria following the Mukden Incident of 1931, though ultimately unable to prevent Japan's withdrawal from the League.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alfred Sao-ke Sze was a pivotal figure in modern Chinese diplomacy, shaping China's engagement with the international community during a period of immense global and domestic upheaval. His persistent advocacy helped establish China's voice on the world stage and contributed to the eventual dismantling of unequal treaties.
